Near Kovno we continued to repulse German attacks on the front west of the Niemen as far as Jessia. The Germans were not successful anywhere except near the village of Codle, where a desperate artillery duel is progressing.

On the front, the Narew and the Bug, the Germans continue persistent attacks, especially on the roads to Lomza, Snidaovo and Kossevo. Further south on the two sides of the K'ev-Malkin Railway our troops Wednesday afternoon were able to assume a counter offensive.

On the roads of the middle Wisla, there has been no change of importance. On the front between the Wieprz and the Bug Wednesday the Germans delivered a series of desperate attacks in the direction of Parczew and on both roads between Cholm and Nladova. All were repulsed with heavy losses to the Germans. These were especially severe east of Ostrow, where the German dead lay in enormous heaps in front of our positions.

On the Bug, the Vistula and the Lota Blpa there has been no essential change.

In the Dniester district, around the mouth of the Stripa, we stopped the Germans' attempt to take the offensive.

The Germans in great force approached simultaneously the entrance of the Gulf of Riga and the Aland skerries Tuesday and beyond. In the area of our warships and shore batteries the German ships rapidly put to sea.

A despatch from Warsaw by way of LODZ, received this afternoon, gives an interesting account of the last hours of Warsaw under the Russians.

Says People Did Not Flee.

The Russian soldiers retired in great haste when the final orders came. They were forced to leave behind them a great number of automobiles they had commandeered and many of the church bells which they intended to take for the bronze and copper in them. The departures on the last two nights, the despatch continues, were entirely military, as a majority of the Poles in the city would not leave and hid to escape deportation.

All knew it was the last night when the reports of the near approach of Prince Leopold from the south became noisied about. The destruction of thirty-two encircling forts began at 11 o'clock and the explosions shook the city. The sky was red with the glare from fires and the three bridges over the Vistula were jammed with soldiers and columns of artillery. There was no intimation of disorder or lack of military discipline at any time.

The ridges were blown up at 1 o'clock in the morning when it became known that the Bavarians had captured the forts in their path. Engineers bombed and mined the middle spans of the structures and at the hour named, they were blown out. However, the piers were not destroyed and the Germans have had little difficulty in erecting new spans or bridging the space with temporary passageways.

It was at 6 o'clock when Russia departed and the city had become Polish for a few minutes again after many years, that an automobile bearing two German officers dashed through the street, its passengers as if they were on a pleasure ride. The machine stopped before the town hall, where a citizens committee, entirely of Poles, came forward to greet the officers. The interchange of courtesies was brief. It was directed that the activities of the city were to continue. Stern reference was made to sniping. Before this conference had ended into the city swept a patrol of lancers, their lances entwined with flowers and all of them singing "Die Wacht am Rhein."

Be it enacted by the legislature of Alabama:

Section 1. All county officers of all counties in Alabama, which now have, or which may hereafter have population of as much as 150,000 people, according to the last federal census, or any such census, which may hereafter be taken, in which circuit court, or court of like jurisdiction is now authorized to be held at a place other than at the county site of such counties for the trial of cases and transaction of business relating thereto, arising within a designated portion of such county, or in which such court may hereafter be authorized by law to be so held, are hereby authorized, directed and required, in addition to their respective offices at the county sites of such counties, to install, keep and maintain offices, as in this act provided, at such place other than at the county sites of such counties for the transaction of all business, executive, ministerial and judicial pertaining to such county offices and officers that arise within the territory within which the cases arising therein may be tried in the circuit court or court of like jurisdiction, held at such place other than at the county site of such counties.

Sec. 2 That all business pertaining to the respective county offices and officers of such counties that arises within the territory within which the cases arising therein may be tried in the circuit court or court of like jurisdiction, held at a place other than at the county site of such counties, shall be transacted at such offices by such officers at such place of holding the court, and all records made thereat shall be kept there, and not elsewhere.

Sec. 3 That there shall be kept at such offices all records, papers and books in all respects similar to the records, papers and books that are required to be kept or may be kept by such officers at their respective offices at the county site.

Sec. 4 That all papers, documents and other things pertaining to the title to that are authorized to be filed and recorded in any office in such county are hereby authorized and required to be filed and recorded in such offices of such officers at such place other than at the county site, as in this act provided for, if the property affected thereby, or sought to be affected thereby, is located or partly within the territory within which the cases arising therein may be tried in the circuit court or court of like jurisdiction, at such place; provided, however, if such property is located partly within such territory, and partly within the remaining territory of such county, then such instrument, document or paper must be filed and recorded both in the office at the county site, and in such office at such place other than the county site as herein provided for; provided further that if such property is located partly within such territory as herein provided for, and partly within some other county, then such instrument, document or paper may be recorded at the place herein provided for, and also in the proper office in the other county. Such records in either of the events in this section provided for shall operate in all respects just as though the same had been filed and recorded in the offices of the respective officers of the county site of such county. Hotel, with maps and oratory, depicted the glories of the route from New Albany to Salem, thence to Seymour and Indianapolis by way of Brownstown.


Perry McCart of Paoli, close ally of Mr. Taggart and Robert Miller of Bloomington, mounted to oratorical heights in supporting their theories that the best route for the Dixie highway from New Albany north is through Paoli, Orleans, Mitchell, Bedford, Bloomington and Martinsville, to Indianapolis. Frank Gardner espoused the cause of Henryville and Scottsburg as the direct line north from Louisville and New Albany to Indianapolis.


W. H. Lincoln of Columbus put up a business man's talk for the Seymour-Columbus route and remained neutral on the Salem and Scottsburg routes. Either way would suit Seymour and Columbus, but Lincoln could not see the Bloomington-Bedford idea. The hottest fight in Indiana is being waged by the factions representing the so-called "airline" route through Lafayette to Chicago and Logansport-South Bend interests.


Congressman Will R. Wood of Lafayette waxed warm in his speech for routing the Dixie highway from Indianapolis through Lebanon, Lafayette, Rensselaer, and Hammond to Chicago, designating it as the "airline" route. W. H. Johnson of Crawfordsville, urged that the road be made to touch at Charlottesville and then proceed northward to Chicago.


Loaded With Maps and Figures.


Rufus McGee, Logansport representative, argued for routing the highway by way of Logansport to South Bend. Milton Kraus of Kokomo urged that the road run northward from Indianapolis through Kokomo and Peru, the route known as the range road. Each speaker presented a mass of figures and maps, each additional exhibit only serving to make the question more puzzling to the commission.


It is expected that the Dixie highway commission will conclude its route fixing labors Saturday, and that the road will be definitely pinned on the map. Michigan's delegation continued its fight Friday for recognition in the commission, but no agreement was reached. Michigan offers to add 400 miles to the Dixie highway if the road is routed through South Bend, but there is a strong faction favoring Chicago as the northern terminal of the thoroughfare.


Kuhns vs. Murdock.


When the commission went to bed last night, following the big parade, there was a confusion of opinions in all their brains. The fact that Indiana has four fights on its hands played a part in the threatened abandonment of the plan to touch Indiana at all. Sam Murdock of Lafayette, representing the Lebanon-Lafayette route, and L. Louis Kuhns of South Bend, had a lively argument over the merits of the two routes, and Murdock, although admitting that he had greater financial interests in South Bend than in Lafayette, stood for the Lafayette route, as he said, for sentiment's sake. He denied having any pecuniary interest in Lafayette.


Murdock's Attitude a Puzzle.


"Why," said Murdock, "the road would not even pass one of our farms in Lafayette district, and we have large holdings in traction stock at South Bend." Murdock's attitude was a puzzle to Kuhns, and he frankly told him so. Yet Murdock clung to the old home town, Lafayette. He now lives in Indianapolis.


Former Gov. Cox of Ohio, and Carl G. Fisher also had a warm argument over the Indiana-Ohio routes last night, and Fisher accused Cox of not being able to look at the big idea in building national highways by direct routes. The Ohio crowd got out bulletins yesterday, in which they attempted to prove that Chicago was almost a hundred miles nearer the Gulf of Mexico by way of Cincinnati than by way of Louisville. Fisher defied them to prove the statement. They merely answered the charge with the declaration that the figures merely were estimates.

Nogales, Ariz., Nov. 27.—With the expected arrival here early today of an additional 100 United States infantry to reinforce the troops at the border, residents of this town experienced a feeling of security such as had not been enjoyed since Villa forces took possession of Nogales, Sonora, following their defeat at Agua Prieta.

There was evidence of renewed confidence in every quarter and the belief was generally expressed that there should be no recurrence of excitement. Snipers fired across the border, killing one and dangerously wounding another United States soldier, such an attack.

The troops expected to arrive today will compose a provisional brigade made up from the Seventh and Twentieth United States infantry, stationed at Douglas, Ariz.

Three U. S. Soldiers Shot.
Herbert S. Gates, private in Company L, Twelfth infantry, was most seriously wounded along with two other American soldiers. He was shot in the abdomen. An operation was reported to have resulted satisfactorily and it was believed he had an even chance to recover. Arthur L. Saup, of the same company, was shot in the right foot.

The dead American soldier was Stephen Littles, 20 years old. He also was a member of Company L. Littles was from Fairmont, N. C. He enlisted last February at Columbus.

Eight Looters Executed.
Evidence that any attempt at looting in Nogales, Sonora, during the occupation of that town on the Mexican side of the border by Carranza forces would be summarily dealt with, was conveyed to the American side last night, when Carranza's forces had executed eight alleged looters.

Among the men executed was a Carranza captain, it was said, and three Carranza soldiers. Three other men also were executed.

Drunken Villa Man Starts Fight.
The intoxicated Villa soldier who started the fighting with United States troops was fighting with a woman on the main street of the Mexican town. She tried to take his rifle from him. He snatched it from her grasp, whirled around, and fired directly into a squad of American soldiers on the boundary line, fifty yards away.

This seemed to be a signal for snipers. A moment later bullets began to fly over the line.

The American infantrymen replied. They were ordered, however, to endanger no Mexican who was not actually firing at them.

The first exchange of shots lasted ten or twelve minutes.

Second Brush on Border.
Colonel Sage and his officers remained in complete control of the United States soldiers, who were on guard for more than an hour before the Mexicans again became active.

Then it was noticed that a band of mounted Mexicans were making their way over the hills toward the boundary to the westward of Nogales.

The United States soldiers hurried into action and a few minutes later shots, again, were flying across the border line at Nogales. It was learned that these Mexicans merely were trying to escape from the Mexican town. They were intercepted by the advanced cavalry column of Colonel Cardenas.

To Pursue Villa Forces.
Gen. Alvaro Obregon, whose Carranza forces occupied Nogales, Sonora, yesterday after Villa snipers had exchanged shots with United States troops, was preparing today to take the field in an effort to run down the remaining Villa forces who fled from the town.

Reports today said General Dieguez, in command of the Carranza forces defending Hermosillo, capital of Sonora, had sent soldiers northward from that city.

General Obregon, it was said, hoped to corner Villa soldiers by sending a column from Nogales.

Early today a work train was dispatched from Nogales to Hermosillo to repair the tracks damaged yesterday when the Villa forces evacuated the town.

Herbert Gates, private of Company L, Twelfth infantry, seriously injured in the fighting yesterday, rallied well today after an operation last night.

sleeves of 1845, she may choose these
for her garden party frocks, or she may
wear ruffles to the waist like the war
time ladies of 1860. Grass and trees

these variations of feminine fashion, and

into one charming picture in which the
most divergent forms and colors will not
clash.

times they are made to match each other
and worn with a white gown. A cape-
like garment, with two big slits for the
arms, was made of black and white toile
de Jouy, as the French call cretonne,
lined with bright green. The hat was a
large round sailor, made of the same
material, and trimmed with a green rib-
bon, which ran around the crown and
hung down behind in two long streamers.

same shade was carried, and the gown
was of ruffled white organdie, the ruff-
les all edged with plain black footing.

on with green ribbons completed the care-
fully thought-out costume.

of the utmost fragility may be chosen if
one likes. The creasing and crumpling
of travel need not be considered. Best
of all, adequate laundry facilities are al-
ways at hand. Freshness is the quality
most to be desired in all summery cos-
tumes.

cently with charming effect. Fluffy

above them. All the guests were furnished

dancing began it was a pretty sight to
see the couples weaving in and out and
the brightly colored globes following
their movements in the air above them.

A new Mexican crisis looms on the
horizon today.

If General Carranza doesn't soon

if you don't know any more than

Stafford is now the county seat of
Graham county and the average citizen
knows who the men are who worked
and done everything in their power to
make Stafford the county seat.


The campaign for the county seat
was turned over to the board of direc-
tors of the Stafford Chamber of Com
merce, and Joe Sullivan was elected as
secretary to the campaign committee
by the citizens of Stafford at a mass
meeting that was held for that purpose.


How well the Stafford Chamber of
Commerce board of directors attended
to the task imposed upon them by the
citizens of Stafford may be Judged by
the election returns and by the large
majority that Stafford won on June
10Th.


The average man knows but little of
the large amount of work that was
done by those men who labored night
and day and spent their money freely
on everything that would help to bring
the county seat to Stafford, where it
belongs. 1t is well known truth that
it is impossible to satisfy everyone, yet
it is possible to satisfy the majority.


The correspondence file of the Stafford
Chamber of Commerce is open to the
public and it is, indeed, a narrow man,
who after reading over the many letters
of inquiries, some for honey, wheat,
eggs. corn, fruit, land, business oppor-
tunities, ETC., that can then say that
the Stafford Chamber of Commerce has
not accomplished what it set out to do.


A live town, something doing all the
time, is the slogan of the Stafford Cham
Der of Commerce board of directors
and it is to be regretted that some of
our local live wires do not keep in touch
with the affairs of the organization,
but condemn publicly something that
most well-known citizens have approved.


The secretary is in position to be
criticised for everything that he under
takes to do, and in order to be sure
that he is right before doing anything,
he always secures the opinion of the
board of directors and then proceeds to
carry out orders. Therefore, next time
you hear some one protest against
wrestling match, or some other celebra-
tion that the committee has seen fit to
arrange for, please remember that Joe
Sullivan is only obeying the orders of
those who have such affairs in charge.


The Stafford Chamber of Commerce

Despite the fact that Mr. Quigg insisted that he had not raised the point the convention adjourned until Monday after a roll call ordered by President Root, showed only 10 of the 165 delegates present.

Up to the time of adjournment the one section of the judiciary article, leaving but seven sections to be considered on Monday, including those providing for Children's Courts, exemptions from jury duty, the selection of Commissioners of Jurors in counties and recognizing the Torrens system of land titles.

Republican Leader Wickersham served notice that he would ask the Committee on Rules to bring in a rule limiting debate hereafter in order that the convention could complete its work in time.

For Elective Magistrates.

City Magistrates may be elected to Brooklyn borough if the new Constitution is adopted by the people and the Legislature passes a law to that effect, according to an amendment inserted to-day in the judiciary article.

The amendment was offered by James R. Latson of Brooklyn and was adopted by a vote of 15 to 20, with 10 delegates. The Brooklyn Republicans delegates joined the upstate Republican delegates in helping them amend the article so as to keep the justices of the peace practically as they are and the upstate delegates reciprocated by aiding the Brooklyn Republicans carry their amendment for elective Magistrates in any borough which the Legislature may determine.

The Brooklyn Magistrates are now appointed by the Mayor.

"This should not be done," declared L. Nancey Nicoll in discussing the Latson amendment. "Why should there be a different rule in Brooklyn borough? Does Brooklyn want to secede? Why should they set themselves up separately? The Borough of Manhattan would be glad to have her."

Brooklyn now pays about 2 per cent of the taxes of the city, and the main burden falls upon the residents of Manhattan. I had supposed that the Borough of Brooklyn, which had succeeded in annexing itself to the city of New York and in compelling the old city to pay 2 per cent of the taxes of the greater city, was satisfied with the bargain.

The little folks of Pine Bluff learned with great pleasure yesterday that the Big Brothers are on the job, and as a result, there are no children in this city and immediate section who fear they will be missed.

As scientific studies show that children, in the depths of their hearts, believe in the Big Brothers and Santa Claus, one little girl at the court house was heard to remark that she hoped "the Big Brothers will bring Johnny a pair of shoes and stockings, like they did last year, because he won't have any." To the children, such necessities appear to be classed as luxuries, and they are deeply grateful, much more grateful than are many grown-ups for whom favors or courtesies are shown.

Miss Julie Houston, secretary of the Associated Charities, who is compiling the name of the tots who are likely to be visited by Santa Claus, believes there will be more such children this year than was the case last year. This means we must be more Big Brothers. The good news was received yesterday by the Big Brothers and Miss Houston, that the folks are going to continue their custom of distributing toys and goodies to the poor children. This will help materially in caring for all the tots. But there are so many of the tots to be cared for, that there must be a host of Big Brothers.

Beginning Monday, the Big Brothers are expected to call Miss Houston by phone, or see her, that the list of children might be distributed among the Big Brothers. Each Big Brother is expected to serve as Santa Claus for at least one child. He can care for more, if he desires to do so. If he wants, Miss Houston will arrange to deliver the stuff to the home of the child, or the Big Brother himself can have that pleasure, as it is up to him. All that he is asked to do, is to provide the means of making at least one child happy this Christmas.

There is one man in Pine Bluff who is a real Big Brother. He knows of his own experience the mass of sorrow suffered by a little fellow who gets nothing from Santa Claus on Christmas Day. He himself, was a "poor kid" with all child's belief in the goodness of Santa Claus. But he woke up one Christmas morning, to find not only that his stocking was empty, but that there was hardly more than crust in the house for his mother, his brothers and sisters, and himself. This happened only once, with that family. But it made that man a Big Brother.

Springfield Republican.

A vivid picture of and tribute to the women of France is given in a letter from Raymond Sabours, the great specialist to Springfield physician. It is written under date of Paris June 20, as follows:

One result of the war has been the disappearance from the streets of certain types of women, and Paris today has taken the aspect that Parisians used to qualify provincial. Everyone goes about his business there; manifestations of neither joy nor sorrow, the general impression given is that there are duties to be done, and that the people are doing them. There are no balls, receptions; the theaters little patronized, vanity and worldliness have disappeared. The old relations no longer exist; what remains are dinners of family intimates, and such each brings and each contributes his news, his opinions, his hopes of the future. The men, skilled with their fingers, only talk and listen; the women in addition to these abilities excel in needlework, and crochet, making articles for soldiers and prisoners. Those who have sons at the front work for them; those who without sons have constituted themselves godmothers to orphan soldiers from lists furnished for that purpose. And the great joy of such reunions is the reading of a diary which some woman has got from her husband at the front.

It was at such a reunion the other evening and I listened to the reading of the diary of a friend, Major G. It contained forty pages, closely written, without punctuation, soiled and difficult to read. But what an evening it was! The simple story of a doctor sent from Paris to Mans and thence to Chartres; from Chartres to Rheims, the Marne and to Belgium and then the long and painful retreat back to the Marne; up again and advance, without chance of repose, to arrive exhausted in the Argonne, sent to the rear with his ambulance for rest; they had just arrived when the order came to again forward, and for twelve days he was present at continuous fighting at Albert and Lassigny. Just one thing the diary did not say, namely that he had been mentioned in the order of the day and decorated for decision and energy. His wife was part of the party, a mother of three children; maybe she skipped a thread during the reading but her hands never stopped.

I can tell you a few more examples of feminine fortitude, you, dear friend, who know the French women—at least you know some of them. The true French, that the casual stranger never knows, for though they have not the gynaceum of the ancients, they have an exclusiveness, a seclusion of family almost equal to theirs; to the stranger in general, to the stranger of every country, the real French woman is an unknown creature. And hence has arisen the native yet grotesque belief accepted that the French type of woman is to be found in pleasure resorts. We suffer, as the Greeks suffered, for two other reasons: the one because, like theirs, women are fair, and to the traveller supposed to be the other, because, like them, artistic, and to the ignorant of all lands the artistic is voluptuous.

Another of the party that evening, Madame S., has two sons at the front; one, Bernard, belonging to a regiment of 5000, of whom but seventeen are left. A short while ago with the cunning of a fox she penetrated the lines up to the heights of Abbovie, determined to see her Bernard before he, too, might join his comrades. She told us her own Odyssey; how she got past the lines to be later sent back, another attempt and arrested, and finally with the help of several shrewd peasants and ruined highways, she reached her destination and as she told us, all was wonderful and she knitted grew apace.

At another such gathering of friends there was among us a Mademoiselle B., young, whose father and brother are fighting in the Vosges; she almost blew in us from Rheims, for one can't telegraph from Rheims what story she had to tell. Leaving the Mediterranean at the outbreak of the war, to offer her services to her friend, the superintendent of the Rheims hospital, she witnessed the grief of the German invasion, and the joy of the French return after the Marne. She lived among the wounded during 100 days of ceaseless bombardment; at Christmas time set up Christmas trees in the cathedral cellars for orphan children. I tell you, my friend, American womanhood couldn't show anything beat this radiant young creature, alert and vigorous, who had spent the winter almost outdoors, for there was not a pane of glass left in her windows. As contrasting experiences she told of a shell that fell on her empty bed, scattering a rain of pillow feathers to the court, but alas, the next one killed six poor wounded devils nearby. As showing that French gaiety can rise above every gloom, she said that her favorite practical joke to initiate, by a screech whistle, the noise of arriving shells, and then laugh at the prudent colleague who threw himself on his stomach. And, my friend, there is no laugh more justified, more true, than his who does his duty in dread surroundings. She gave my children a bag of shrapnel balls which, she said, the children of Rheims use as marbles.

I had at St. Louis recently another type, a French Protestant, stern and puritanical, who wore enormous spectacles, and never travelled without a Bible under her arm. Her wrist had been broken and a piece of her arm carried away, but she wouldn't await complete restitution to hurry back to the front.

An aged lady from Versailles of those old aristocrats of infinite distinction, bringing a daughter who had broken down under the strain of ambulance work. In interrogation I found she had six sons under the flag, the seventh being still too young, but intending to join three months hence. Of the six, one was killed at Chareroi; two disappeared during those dreadful days of retreat which you remember, lasted from August 7 to 20. She is being nursed at home for a dreadful laceration of the thigh, the other two being well and in the heat of things at Alsace. And she told her story very quietly, neither boastfully nor in despair, without tears, without melodrama—just simply. Alas! I could tell you a couple more patients, victims of brutality or worse, but what's the use of relating horrors? I know of fashionable women who spend their nights in the stations, serving soup or coffee to the passing wounded; and of one in particular, who among the wounded found her own husband taken to a distant hospital, and who she must let pass while she bravely waited the next convoy.

My dear friend, how can one not be proud of these women who fill such roles? And calmly, uncomplainingly, and with constancy! And their heroism isn't limited to war alone; won't know our hospitals, all men.

A detailed account of President Wilson's relations with the Chevy Chase Club is given in a letter written by A. S. Worthington, Washington attorney and member of the board of governors of the club, and printed in the New York Sun this morning. The letter was prompted, Mr. Worthington says, by erroneous statements which have been printed regarding the President declining an honorary membership in the club.

As a matter of fact, President Wilson has been an honorary member of the Chevy Chase Club since March 1913, although he did decline such membership when rendered him a month previous.

Gives the Facts.

Color has been lent the reports that the President was not a member of the Chevy Chase Club because of the fact that he seldom plays golf on that course, preferring the links of the Washington Country Club, at Jewell Va., which he uses almost daily when in Washington.

The letter of Mr. Worthington to the Sun reads:

To the Editor of the Sun.

Sir: In the Sun of yesterday it was stated that President Wilson declined an honorary membership in the Chevy Chase Club. As similar statements have been made in many newspapers, it is desirable that all the facts regarding that matter should be made known. As a member of the club and quoting from the minutes of its board of governors, I therefore give you the facts and ask you to publish them.

On February 10, 1913, the board tendered honorary membership in the club to Mr. Wilson. On February 15, 1913, Mr. Wilson declined to accept the membership rendered, giving as reason that it would be practically impossible for him to avail himself of the courtesy of the club because of the absolute engrossment of public duties.

Reconsidered Declination.

Immediately after his Inauguration through Henry Clay Stewart, of this city, who was then president of the local association of Princeton Alumni, President Wilson informed the board of governors of the club that he wished to reconsider his declination of membership in the club. This intimation was submitted to the board at a regular meeting held on March 10, 1913. Thereupon a resolution was adopted by the board authorizing the president of the club, Mr. Thomas Hyde, to see President Wilson and confer upon him honorary membership if he desires to accept it, and to tender to him active membership if preferred.

At the next meeting of the board which was held on March 24, 1913, Mr. Hyde reported to the board that Mr. Wilkins (a member of the board) himself called on President Wilson at his solicitation and extended to him honorary membership in the club, which he accepted.

The membership which the President so accepted he still retains. The members of his family, who are privileged guests by virtue of his membership, have been frequent visitors at the club.

A. S. WORTHINGTON.

TO CORRESPONDENT OF THE SUN—"A. O." writing from Boston on the conditions on the Williamsburg Bridge says:

I am positive that the work on the north roadway of the WILLIAMSBURG Bridge could be finished up in five days; and it has now been going on weeks and is not near completion.

The work on the Williamsburg Bridge to which attention is called is roadway repairing. The condition of the pavement on the approaches of this bridge makes necessary the complete replacement of approximately one-half or thus roadway width, an area of 10,150 square yards. Of this an area of 3,056 square yards has been repaired. The work has been and is being expedited in every way consistent with a minimum of inconvenience to traffic and a minimum cost to the department.

In connection with the roadway repairs it is necessary to renew expansion joints, which in this case are made of steel. This work can only be done after the old pavement has been taken up and before any concrete or any new blocks have been set in place as I believe, has given your correspondent a false idea of the time required to do this work.

Let me call attention at this time to my dissatisfaction with the roadway conditions on the Williamsburg Bridge and also on the Brooklyn and Queensboro bridges. It is my entire conviction that the roadways of these bridges should all be repaved, and a programme covering the entire work is now being worked out in this department. This programme has not yet been presented either to the Board of Estimate and Apportionment or to the Mayor in full and comprehensive fashion, although the department has, from time to time, pointed to the necessity of repaving the bridge roadways in such a manner as to reduce the present heavy repair and maintenance costs.

The capitalization of this programme has been deferred solely because of the stringency of municipal funds, but it is my belief that money for this substantial improvement should be appropriated in view of the public convenience it would afford, and of the fact that it would pay for itself very rapidly in diminished yearly expenditure. I am now having prepared charts showing the heavy maintenance costs of the roadways for several years back, and it is my hope that these figures will be sufficiently convincing to induce the Board of Estimate to feel that this is an expenditure fully worthy of consideration even at a time when all expenditures of city funds are being subjected to the closest scrutiny.

Referring generally to the roadway problem, I would say that it is my intention to replace the present roadway planking of the Brooklyn Bridge with wood block. Experiments with blocks of various kinds have demonstrated that the proper pavement will be creosoted wood block on an untreated timber under deck. The replacement of this structure with wood block will mean a saving of many thousands of dollars yearly in repairs and maintenance, as well as eliminating the constant interference of traffic that these repairs occasion.

On the Queensboro Bridge a difficult problem has confronted the department. The pavement on the greater part of the bridge, in fact on all of this bridge with the exception of the Manhattan approach and part of the Queens approach, has failed completely. The failure has been primarily due to the lack of proper foundation and to the increased vehicle loads that this bridge now accommodates. Several experiments made by the department have proved to my satisfaction that the proper foundation has been found by replacing the present Medina sandstone blocks with granite blocks. Medina block is a very soft stone and some of the blocks have shown a reduction in depth of over four inches due to wear. One of my first acts in coming into the department was to issue orders that no more Medina stone should be used on this bridge and that granite blocks be substituted.

When the letter of "A. O." was called to my attention I called for a special report on the progress of the roadway work, and also had the work inspected and checked up by the Chief Engineer. The reports of the engineer in charge, and of the Chief Engineer of the department are quite convincing as setting the question that a work presenting many difficulties is being prosecuted with intelligence and economy.

J. L. BRACKK,
Commissioner, Department of Bridges.

The decision is believed to reach "grandfather clause" legislation in many southern states.

To Cities in Maryland.

The mental alteration

With every sad gradation,
Of maniac desperation:-

And utter condemnation

Why sanction its duration,
Or show disapprobation
Or any combination
For its determination?
We deem a declaration
That offers no temptation
By any palliation
Of this abomination,
The only sure foundation;

For in participation
With this association,
You may by meditation
Insure the preservation
Of a future generation
From all contamination
And may each indication
OF such regeneration
Be the theme of exultation
Till its final consumation.

and Roumania are near to making the

motives actuating these nations is
the fear that Germany and Austria
will win. They are convinced that the
defeat of the allies would be a mis-
fortune for themselves. They are
frankly afraid of the central Euro-
pean powers and the loss of all

be followed by aggressions against

methods of Germany in the past year

call the roll of Roumania, Bulgaria,

finding to-day one dependable friend.

To the Editor of The Age Herald:

A very great calamity is impending over Birmingham in the apparent certainty that the presbytery of north Alabama will condemn the teaching of the pastor of the South Highlands Presbyterian church. None can deplore this more than I. It seems to me an even greater calamity for that whole denomination than for Birmingham, or for the beloved pastor.

Every little while a man is born who cannot help framing his own theology. The great majority accept the most contiguous orthodoxy, but this man is driven to phrase for himself what his soul reports to him of self and mankind and God. In these days a new orthodoxy has been growing, and the men who make it are of the Edmonds type. A church framed upon definite theological propositions is certain to evolve tradition of interpretation to accompany those propositions. The new type of orthodoxy must either seek another church fellowship or compel a change in the interpretation or in the propositions, or in both.

Other groups of Presbyterians have enlarged their traditional interpretations or have modified their theological statements and so are keeping their progressive minds in their ministry. It seems most unlikely that the southern Presbyterian body will follow this path. And what a pity it is! It would be absurdly presumptuous in me most respectfully to urge upon the North Alabama presbytery to petition the general assembly to proceed at an early date in such modifications as would make room for such men in its pastoral service.

And yet why not? It has been my lot to hear nearly all the greatest preachers of Professionalism within the past 40 years. From childhood onwards, I go on record as saying that this man belongs in the first rank. His message gets its unction from his deep personal knownship with God. His voice, his presence, his simplicity, his sanity, his style and his dramatic fitness are consolidated with the finest qualities of character and feeling. In the best sense of those words I know him to be both evangelical and orthodox. Whatever happens Birmingham must not lose him. Whatever happens there is no blame to be placed on those who do not agree with him and who adjudge him unorthodox with the traditions and theological propositions that began to shape themselves 300 or 400 years ago. It would be to the great gain of the church to keep such man as Dr. Edmonds in a position of leadership. But to do so she must qualify her past deliverances, and that is very hard to hope for. My sympathy is with the pastor, the church and the presbytery for they are facing a problem created by these modern days, their life and need.

GEORGE EAVES.

Birmingham, October 15, 1915

New York, May 21.—The Rockefeller Foundation has received information that conditions in that part of Russian Poland within the German and Austrian lines are much worse than in Belgium or northern France and that the population is now actually starving.

The Foundation today received cables from its war relief commissioners, Ernest P. Bicknell and Eliot Wadsworth, saying that they had made a careful review of the situation in Poland east of the fighting line, including Galicia and of the Warsaw district. The most urgent need for outside aid is for the relief of the Jewish population.

If the 12 months of fighting in Europe have brought no decision, neither have 12 months of warning to the United States produced any tangible result. To-day the American army and navy stand about where they did at the outbreak of the conflict. The army is still an immobile skeleton; the law is still lopsided and lacking both equipment and men. A ship or two authorized in the regular run of business has been launched, and it is announced that some modern submarines are to be built but this is only playing at preparedness.

The brighter side to the picture of the loss of a year is the increasing evidence that the period of mere agitation has passed and that the Government is finally waking to an understanding of its preparedness, and both the Secretary of War and the Secretary of the Navy have let it be known that they will submit constructive programs to the next Congress. Perhaps it may not be possible to move more quickly than this, but there should at least be no time lost unnecessarily. For, as the motto at the head of the leader in the current Proceedings of the United States Naval Institute eloquently puts it: "Too late on earth may be too soon in hell."

Washington, Aug. 12.—President Wilson on his return from Chamiss, today, was given a comprehensive account of the Mexican situation by Secretary Lansing.

The secretary told the president that official reports indicated that the situation in the vicinity of Brownsville was of a local character and that quiet prevailed at Vera Cruz, where there had been some anti-foreign demonstrations. He outlined in detail the discussion of peace plans at the New York conference yesterday of the American diplomats.

Situation Not Alarming.

Neither the president nor Secretary Lansing was inclined to view the situation as requiring any further precautionary measures than have been Mexican waters and more federal troops to the Texas border. They devoted most of their time to a discussion of the Inter-American plan on which they are basing their hopes for the early restoration of peace in Mexico.

The appeal to all factions has not yet been sent, although signed by Secretary Lansing and the ambassadors of South American governments participating in the conference. A list of chiefs, generals and governors is being compiled and as soon as the locations of all are determined that appeal will be telegraphed simultaneously to every part of Mexico.

Carranza Holds, Out. —

On the eve of this action came the announcement from the Villa agency here tonight that General Carranza had flatly refused to enter into any peace conference and would not treat with his opponents. Enrique C. Llorente, Washington representative of General Villa, gave out letters which had passed between him and Eliseo Arredondo, the Carranza representative here. Mr. Llorente began the correspondence on observing in the press that Charles A. Douglas, counsel for General Carranza, had filed a brief with the State Department calling attention to the presence in Washington of Luis Cabrera and Eliseo Arredondo as Carranza representatives and saying that either or both of them, I am assured, will be glad to confer with any element of the Mexican people with a view to furthering the welfare of the nation.

Carranza Will Not Recognize Villa.

Mr. Llorente promptly telegraphed General Villa and was instructed to begin discussion of peace terms. Mr. Arredondo too replied that he would refer the matter to General Carranza, whose response today came in the form of instructions to Arredondo not to enter into negotiations with the Villa agents. After stating that he would accept only the unconditional surrender of his opponents, the Carranza message set forth that there could be no negotiations with the Villa forces because their troops on July 11 last attacked a military convoy train, killing many innocent people. Mr. Llorente declared tonight that Mr. Douglas' statement was made several weeks after this incident was alleged to have occurred.

Villa Willing to Sign Armistice.

Incidentally Secretary Lansing revealed today that General Villa had recently informed the State Department that he was willing to sign an armistice for three months or a longer period during which peace conference might be held. Mr. Llorente confirmed this information and added that General Felipe Angeles was now in conference with General Villa at Chihuahua relative to details of such an armistice. He pointed to this meeting as an evidence of harmony in the Villa ranks.

Villa and Zapata Willing.

Indications are that the Villa and Zapata elements are preparing to receive favorably the appeal of the United States and the Latin-American governments. They already are planning a peace conference.

Officials of the American government hoped that many generals reported to be partisans of Carranza ultimately will give their adherence to a peace conference. WASHINGTON. Nov. 12.—William J. Bryan, in a letter to Colonel Robert N. Thompson, president of the Navy league, today repudiated statements credited to him in his speech at Philadelphia on Nov. 3, to the effect that the Navy league is subsidized by munition-making concerns. NEW YORK, April 19.—Heavy profit taking caused a sharp reaction in the market just before the close, after a broad active day, in which the railroads were the leaders, making the largest gains as well as being the most wanted, both by traders and outsiders. United States Steel, which was one of the strong issues of this morning, led the fall, losing nearly three points from the close of Saturday, before any supply orders were put out. The rest of us, followed the lead of Steel, and virtually everything on the list went off. This setback was the most vigorous since the upward movement began. Transactions in the loan crowd indicated a material decrease in the short interest and the market felt the lack of this support.

The accumulation of buying orders was evident at the opening. The most prominent and encouraging feature was the diversion of both speculative and professional interest to the standard issues, especially trunk line railroad shares in particular, and brisk upturns occurred throughout this group. Very little in strength was shown in the specialties, which have been unprecedentedly strong for some time past.

RAIDERS argued that the swinging of interest from the specialties, or war stocks, to the standard group was a good sign, and materially helped the technical position of the market. Among the reasons advanced for the strength in the railroad branch was better earnings, brought about by the granting of the 3 per cent. rate advance by the Interstate Commerce Commission, and the gradual and steady betterment in business conditions throughout the country, as indicated by weekly and daily reports.

Trading was on a heavy scale throughout the morning session. Business was at the rate of 100,000 shares for the five hour session, or the largest in many months if not years. As the morning wore on there was no indication that business was diminishing, nor that outside interest was falling off.

Virtually all the railroad issues were up from one to over three points before noon. Reading, for which there was large demand, advanced 2 points; Lehigh Valley, 1; Union Pacific, nearly 2; Chesapeake and Ohio, 1 1/2; Northern Pacific, over 1/2. New York Central, nearly 1. Other less prominent railroad shares were also up, but not as much. Canadian Pacific moved up 1/2 points and Baltimore and Ohio rose 3 points.

United States Steel also became prominent, advancing over a point in the early session. There was a reiteration of the rumor that the company had received a large war order, and that in any event it will supply the raw material to other concerns which have received orders. Then too, the steel trade is gradually becoming better, and mills are reported to be operating on a larger scale. The Gary mill of the Steel Corporation, is said to be working nearly 100 per cent.

Equipment stocks were supplied at concessions, New York Air Brake being the largest loser, dropping 2 points before midday. American Locomotive and Baldwin were also about 1 point lower.

Doheny, president of the company, that arrangements had been completed with important British interests for formation of an English company to handle a considerable proportion of output of Mexican Petroleum Company in the foreign market. He says that in reality they are overpaid and to sustain this charge says that they are receiving from the government amounts which, for hauls of any considerable length, exceed by about two to one the amounts they receive from the express companies for like and similar services.

The dignity and prestige of the Cabinet Office of which Mr. Burleson is the present incumbent assures his hearing before the public and a large degree of credence, because of the natural assumption that judicial attitude will be retained by sworn public official, and that the responsibility he assumes in making any public assertion will be appreciated at least by himself.

Mr. Burleson bases his assertion regarding the mail and express earnings of the railroads upon a number of comparisons of which this is typical:

He says that from New York to Chicago, railway mail pay amounts to $5.20, a portion of the first-class express rate between those cities is approximately 81.20 per 100 pounds.

Not one citizen in thousand would ever suspect that this meant anything except that the railroads carry express matter from New York to Chicago for an average rate of only $1.00 per 100 pounds. The fact is, however, that the express rate Mr. Burleson names is not an average, or in any way representative rate, but is the railroads share of the express company's charge for single 100 pound package, on which the very lowest wholesale rate per pound is given to the shipper. The railroads are paid approximately half the express company's charge.

The railroads receipts from the smaller express packages which make up the great bulk of the actual business and hence their average receipts per 100 pounds of express are far higher than the figure Mr. Burleson quotes, a fact of which it is scarcely conceivable he could be unaware.

VS. James E. Hogan, Executor.


Rescript, Spear, J.


As appears by the agreed statement,
this is an action on an account annexed
brought by Vernon D. Coombs against
the goods and estate of Hannah B. Ho-
gan, late of Bath, in the county of Sag-
adahoc.


As appears by the writ, the officer
was directed to attach the goods and
estate which were of Hannah B. Ho-
gan, late of Bath, in the county of Sag-
adahoc and State of Maine, deceased,
in the possession of James E. Hogan
of said Bath, executor of the last will
and estate of said Hannah B. Hogan,
to the value of one thousand dollars,
and summon the said defendant in his
said capacity as executor.


A special appearance in this action
was entered by attorneys for the ex-e-
cutor of the last will and testament
of Hannah B. Hogan, who as it also
appears by the agreed statement is
James E. Hogan, of Portsmouth, in the
state of New Hampshire.


The first question at issue under the
agreed statement, is whether any de-
fendant is named in the writ. We are
unable to discover any good reason why
there is not. A reading of the declara-
tion does not leave the least doubt upon
the mind, that the plaintiff has sued
the executor of the estate for all
due from the estate to the plaintiff.
No misunderstanding regarding this
question seems possible. The objec-
tion therefore to the form of the plead-
ing is purely technical and, if sus-
tained, must be for want of statutory
requirement in the pleading. The stat-
ute simply provides that an executor
may be sued, but prescribes no form
of action.


The first inquiry to be made is, is an
executor, in an action against him, a
defendant? An affirmative answer is
irresistible. The estate is in the hands
of the executor. He is the only person
against whom an action is authorized
or can be instituted for claim against
the decedent. Where only one executor
is named, he alone is the only indivi-
dual who can represent the estate, who
can sue and be sued in such case.


The executor and the person
named as executor, are always one and
the same. If the executor is a de-
fendant, the person named as execu-
tor is the same defendant.
The second question raised by the
defendant is without merit in accord-
ance with the stipulations.
Case remanded to nisi for trial.
Received October 21, 1915.

and see Eleanor yourself Saturday
tell her how I feel about it. Say that

Madison—The senate of the legislature confirmed the appointment of George Hambrecht of Grand Rapids as member of the state industrial commission, Barney Moran of Rhinelander as state oil inspector and Senator L. G. Kellogg of Rhone as a member of the civil service commission. The senate killed the proposed home rule for cities amendment to the constitution.

The university appropriation bill has gone through both houses of the legislature reduced approximately 100,000 from the amount recommended by the Joint committee on finance. The bill as amended carries a total appropriation of $5,228,000. It went through the senate after sharp debate but received only short consideration in the assembly where the amended bill passed by vote of 75 to 11.

Final action was taken on the normal school appropriation measure which carries $2,650,991. The measure was long debated in the senate but only a slight amendment running all appropriations to the state board of education, newly created body, was incorporated.

Interesting in this connection is the long debate held in the assembly, occupying nearly an hour, over a bill of 1888. The measure was finally passed. As the session nears its close of active work the utmost of good feeling prevailed among the members. While it will still be a week before final adjournment can be had, the actual work of the session has practically been completed. Concurrence was given to senate bill remodeling and codifying all the state fish and game laws. This measure when approved by the governor will make it possible to have all the fish laws published in pamphlet form so that every person will be correctly informed as to the exact status of the laws in force.

Governor Philip has vetoed the bill passed at this session of the legislature for the printing and distributing of 4,000 copies of the Wisconsin blue book biennially. The governor points out that blue books cost the state 60 cents per copy and that the number of additional volumes authorized by the bill would cost the state large sum of money. The old law provided for a liberal distribution of blue books to schools to members of the legislature and to public officials, and the governor sees no reason for increasing the number for distribution. The veto of the governor was sustained.

The Milwaukee sewage problem received final consideration by the legislature and the assembly concurred in the Martin bill providing for bond issue and small mill tax levy to take care of the inauguration of this $1,600,000 project. Throughout the session the proposal has had the opposition of the Socialist party. The assembly killed the Hanson bill limiting the time under which actions may be brought in breach of promise actions and alienation of affections to one year. Assemblyman Reringer's bill for county auditor in Milwaukee county was taken from the table, amended and passed under suspension of the rules.

Mihills, Fond du Lac; H. T. Wilson, Wausau; J. J. Roe, Stanley; Robert McDowell, Oconomowoc; Edward J. Roche, Fennimore; H. S. Griswold, West Salem.

The senate concurred in the La Dain plumbing bill by a vote of 30 to 1, reversing its former position on the bill. The measure extends the scope of the present act. Theodore Roosevelt, when President, was a great believer in the submarine. He was undoubtedly the first, and possibly the only, head of a great nation to take a trip in a submarine. Certainly other presidents, kings or emperors thought of such an adventure at that early stage of the submarine.

No doubt his trip would have remained secret for a time at least, but for the combination of a girl, young reporter, pair of white duck trousers, rainy day and thirsty sailor. The girl was the magnet that drew the young reporter from his post of duty at Oyster Bay to New York. The white ducks were worn by the reporter because the day promised to be warm. The rain came later to confound the wearer of the ducks and the sailor was thirsty because the grape juice administration had not yet come on the scene.

The Plunger, now the A-1, our first submarine, was sent to Oyster Bay to be inspected by President Roosevelt during the summer of 1905. Lieutenant Evans, son of Fighting Bob, was in command. The reporters at Oyster Bay got word that the President planned to make a trip in the Plunger. The President denied most emphatically that he had any such intention. But the reporters were instructed by their newspapers to watch the Plunger. They worked in relays, and from early morning until dusk patrolled the bay and kept a sharp watch for visitors to the submarine. This duty was performed for a week. Because the city council, at it's meeting Monday night, failed to amend the present ordinance fixing the annual tax on telephone and tele- graph poles at $1 per pole, and be- cause the tax will become due June l, City Collector William V. Hut will be called upon to issue notice to the telephone and telegraph companies to pay the tax of $1 per pole.

 Such was the condition which faced the members of the council when they discussed the proposition Monday night, and the condition continues to exist The tax for the new fiscal year becomes due June i. The coun- cil will not meet until June [, unless a special session is held Hence, it will be impossible for the council to make a ch9nge in the tax rate on the poles, until after the tax is due and the call for it's payment has been made by the collector.

 The council Monday night passed a resolution instructing that an ordi- nance be prepared making the tax rate on telegraph and telephone poles for the new year 73 cents per pole This ordinance is expected to be of fered and acted upon at the next reg ular meeting of the council, but in the meantime the tax as at present in effect will become due and Col 1ector Hut, under the law, can do nothing except issue call for it's payment

 Expect Another Compromise.

 While none of those interested ill the matter, will make definite state- ment to this effect, it appears to be the opinion among them that the matter will be amicably adjusted and without loss of time.

 The matter, it is expected, will be adjusted along lines approXimating the following:

 Collector Hut will issue his call for the payment of the tax at the eX- isting tax rate of $1 per pole. The companies, having thirty days or so in which to pay the tax, will bring the matter up at the session of the council on June '. or some member of the council will bring it np, or it will come ilp with the introduction of the ordinance fixing the tax at 75 cents There will be some discussion. One or two members of the council will likely insist on the rate being 7o cents at least: But a motion to amend by making the rate 90 cents will be offered, will be seconded and adopt ed, and then the amended ordinance will be passed. By agreement, the collector will be instructed to accept the new rate of 50 cents per pole, instead of the $1 per pole.

He insisted that when the companies settled on com promise of 75 cents per pole last year, it was .withe the distinct and clear understanding that the rate would be placed at 50 cents again

"The enemy is in your trenches again, Sis!" cried Teddy Herbert to his sister, who had not yet come down to breakfast.


"Dear, dear!" he heard her exclaim, and then he heard hurried footsteps and saw Matte run downstairs, pick up a coat that was lying on a chair in the hall, and slam the front door after her.


Four sixty-foot trenches lay open at the side of the Herbert home, and Matte was running back and forth chasing away the neighbour chickens. The fresh fertilizer which had been placed so carefully in each of the trenches was scattered everywhere, and dismay was written all over the girl's face when she turned to come into the house.


"It's shame!" she said, as she took her place at the table, breathing hard, but looking as fresh as a rose after her exercise in the invigorating March air. "And this one year when I had counted so much on my sweet peas and have followed directions so carefully. What shall I do, mother?"


"Shoot the chickens," suggested Teddy.


"This isn't the war, Teddy," his sister said, squelchingly. "These are sweet pea trenches."


"I'll pass," said Teddy, getting up from the table. "It's not my funeral, Mat. So long!" And with that he was gone.


Matte and her mother were finishing breakfast in silence when they heard the knocker on the front door.


"You go," said Matte, as her mother started to rise.


"I'm George Davis—next door, you know. Just saw you chasing my chickens out of your garden."


"Come in, please," said Matte, opening wide the door to the young man who was introducing himself.


"You see, I've come to stay with my brother, next door, for a while, since my firm saw fit to cut down expenses by letting me out of job. He's never at home and my sister is busy with the baby, so the chickens have been in your trenches owing to folly. I apologize and will swear that it does not happen again."


"Oh, don't worry," Matte hastened to say. "Of course. Well, I have worked so hard this spring, and it does be been rather disconcerting—"


"Disconcerting!" interrupted Davis. "Now that is polite. If I had been in your place I think I would have blessed the whole houseful of neighbors. Your hens!" he laughed.


Matte joined him. "Perhaps I would call it a blessing. I had not thought of it in that light. But so, you won't worry, will you? I'll out this morning and try to plant seeds, and then—"


"Then if my chickens dig them up, I needn't show my face again in the neighborhood?"


Matte nodded, laughing. After more words of apology, George Davis left, and Matte Herbert knew that she liked him and was glad that he was to be her neighbor.


That morning, when she was out of doors, trying to repair the damage done to her trenches, George Davis looked over the hedge which separated the gardens. "It is what I should be doing that," he ventured. "You may help." Matte replied quickly.


A few hours' work with him convinced him that Matte Herbert was not conventional, that she was the most original and charming girl he had met.


Spring came and went, and soon brought the looked-for blossoms to the Herberts' garden. The four feet foot trenches were riot of blooms and some stems held flowers of gigantic proportions.


Matte and her mother and Teddy picked sweet peas each morning, and Matte herself attended to arranging them for the shipping. It was then that her new neighbor called upon her.


"I can't offer you much in return for your help, which I need badly," the girl said, frankly, "but I am still out of position. I could do a small business together with your chickens and our ground."


"I don't need any pay for well run," Davis said earnestly. "I should love to do it."


Later they worked out a scheme for successive raising of table commodities for which they knew of easy and accessible markets. And as they worked on this scheme they fell in love with each other.


One day he told her of his love, of what he had hoped her and him might be.


"My answer is yes, of course," she said. "But we must continue to be partners in business as well as our home. Well, I'm glad the necessity for earning our living together brought you to me and to me you."


"For it was the exigencies of the situation that brought us together."


"It wasn't it," she asked. "It was eyes, it was the enemy in the trenches, dear," he said, laughing, "placing the responsibility."

Bollinger, near Taneytown, was
burned with most of its contents on

the furniture in the lower rooms.

It became known today, however, that there are indications that the new American note to Germany is received in a friendly spirit and there appears no intention further to violate neutral rights on the high seas, the new protest to Great Britain will be despatched probably within the next fortnight.

General Principles.

Data is being gathered at the State Department, but the new note probably will not deal to any extent with specific instances, contending chiefly for the general principles involved with renewed insistence on modifications in the Order-in-Council to conform with what the United States regards as the accepted rules of international law. The recent filing of legal caveat announcing that orders in council and British municipal law do not affect the rights of American citizens under international law was the first step in the policy which the United States is pursuing to obtain acquiescence in its point of view.

Interest centered for the most part today in official and diplomatic quarters on the nature of the new note to Germany. Sufficient of its contents had become known to cause widespread comment on the apparently determined position taken by the United States.

his day. His political enemies named
him the "Undertaker Fox." Among
the political aphorisms attributed to
him was this advice to his son, popu-
larly known as "Prince John": "My
son, never write on political matters,
if you can avoid the necessity by mak-
ing a trip of 50 miles." This was in
stage coach days, when a journey of
50 miles means as much in wasted time
and practically in money cost as a trip
across the continent means today.
Politicians generally have been popu-
larly credited with having taken this
advice to heart and followed it as
closely as possible; but every once in a
while something crops up to show that
the popular impression on this subject
is a delusion. Politicians, like other
people, continue to write letters, and
letters written in the past continue to
appear, occasionally to the confusion
of writers, even when the precaution
has been taken in writing to attach
the injunction: Burn this letter.
Often it is the letter which should have
been burned which is the one and only
one to be retained and to reach ultimate publicity.

After chemical analysis of many plants Brunnich gave the following advice: "All fodder plants related to sorghum must be used with discretion in either the green or dry state and should not be given in large amounts to animals which have tasted for some time." The poison in these plants is hydrocyanic acid. Poisoning usually occurs when the plants have made a stunted growth from drought and are eaten in large quantities, when the animals are very hungry.

Animals poisoned in this way usually die within half an hour and sometimes live only a few minutes. Hydrocyanic acid is the most deadly of poisons and in large doses kills almost instantly. Animals usually die suddenly from paralysis of respiration and before medical measures can be thought of or prepared for use.

From the Pittsburg Dispatch.

The address by President James A. Farrell of the United States Steel corporation before the Engineers society of western Pennsylvania last evening deserves the closest perusal. Its optimism, buttressed by facts and figures, makes it a business tonic.

Such waste pipes shall be so arranged as to admit of frequent flushing, and shall be short as possible, and shall run into an open sink properly trapped.


Drips or Overflow Pipes.


Section 40. All drip or overflow pipes from safes under wash basins, baths, urinals, water closets, or other fixtures shall be by a special pipe run to an open sink, outside of house, or some conspicuous point, and in no case shall any such waste pipe be connected with a soil drain or waste pipe.


Refrigerator Waste Pipe.


Section 41. No waste pipe from a refrigerator or other receptacle in which provisions are kept shall be connected to the sewer.


Number of Water Closets.


Section 42. Each dwelling house shall have at least 1 water closet; dwellings providing for 2 or 3 families must have at least 2 water closets. Hotels, Boarding Houses and buildings where operation of both sexes are employed, separate water closets shall be furnished for men and women.


Water Closets to be Supplied with Water from Flushing Tanks.


Section 43. All water closets within buildings shall be supplied with water from special tanks or cisterns which shall hold not less than eight (8) gallons of water when filled up to level of the overflow pipe for each closet supplied. A group of closets may be on different floors shall not be flushed from one tank, except where a special valve device is used on flush pipe of each water closet, said device shall insure a sufficient water supply and be not subject to syphonic action. On high buildings a house tank shall be erected if so required by the Board of Health. The use of wash out closets is prohibited.


Section 44. No closet, except those placed on the water supply pipes, unless controlled by Johnson valve or its equal, must be equipped with a cast brass flange not less than three sixteenths of an inch in thickness, soldered to lead bend, fitted with a rubber gasket or bolted to the closet.


Yard Water Closets Enclosure.


Section 45. The enclosure of the yard water closet shall be ventilated by slated openings and there shall be a trap door in the floor of sufficient size for access to the hopper trap.


Where Water Closets Shall Not be located.


Section 46. Water closets must not be located in the sleeping apartments of any building nor in any room or apartment which has not direct communication with the exterior of natural air either by window or by air shaft having an area to the open air of at least 4 square feet.


Water Closet Within a Building.


Section 47. All water closets within a building, using lead connection, shall have a cast brass flange not less than three sixteenths of an inch in thickness, soldered on lead bend, fitted with a rubber gasket of sufficient thickness to insure a tight joint.


Rain Water Conductors.


Section 48. Rain conductors shall not be connected to any sewer or drainage system nor used as soil, waste or vent pipe nor shall any soil, waste or air pipe be used as a rain conductor and if placed within a building, shall be cast iron pipe with lead.


Exhaust or Waste.


Section 49. No steam exhaust or waste from steam pipes shall be connected with an house drain, soil pipe or sewer. No sediment pipes from kitchen boilers shall be connected to the sewer.


Section 50. No privy vault or cesspool for sewerage shall hereafter be constructed in any part of the city where a sewer is at all accessible.


Section 51. No connection from any cesspool or privy shall be made with any sewer nor shall any water closet or house drainage empty into cesspool or privy well where sewer is accessible.


Permits may be issued by the Board of Health to waste pipes from buildings to be connected with cesspools constructed for that special purpose, the sides and bottom of the same to be constructed of brick of at least 8 inches thick laid in cement and water tight so that the contents cannot escape therefrom and have tight covers vented and so constructed as to be readily and easily cleaned out. Section 52. When privy well, vault or cesspool is to be abandoned it must be cleaned out by having its contents removed and thoroughly disinfected, and it shall be filled in with fresh earth, and in no case shall privy well, or cesspool be filled in until used contents have been entirely removed and has been inspected and approved by the inspector.


Section 53. In case plumbing or drainage work of any kind shall be constructed or done in violation of the provisions of this ordinance, the same shall be removed or perfected in accordance with this ordinance within 90 days after notice in writing to that effect to the owner or plumber.

Section 55. During construction or building, the contractor shall provide for workmen a privy to be constructed in a sanitary manner and in accordance with a permit issued therefor by the Board of Health.


Section 56. In case where a building is found to be in an unsanitary condition through defective plumbing or otherwise, direction of the Board of Health concerning building changes and repairs shall be complied with within a reasonable time as may be designated.


Section 57. If any section of the above ordinance shall be declared illegal, it shall not affect any other section thereof.


Penalty for Violation.


Section 58. Any person, persons or corporation violating the provisions of any section or sections of this ordinance, shall upon conviction thereof, forfeit and pay a penalty of not less than Ten ($10.00) Dollars nor more than One Hundred ($100.00) Dollars for each and every offense.


Section 59. The Board of Health may hear cause and upon written complaint and after a public hearing revoke, suspend or cancel any plumbers license or permit issued by the Board of Health provided however, if a person or persons, against whom complaint is made.

He opined that these thugs are resented as the people of Georgia and so more harm than good.

MANISTIQUE, Mich. March 14.

Simplifying the present primary and enacting the old party enrollment—a modified form was introduced this morning by Senator Wood of Manistique. The measure to-day is one of 80 bills to be introduced by Manistique solons, two of which in the course of preparation.

Under the terms of the Wood bill, the primary will be set for the second Tuesday in September. The primary will be held at the time under the existing provisions that, when one is registered he must state his party preference.

In a primary election the ballots of each party are printed on separate tickets and, upon presenting himself at the booth and giving his name, the voter is given the ballot of the party to which he is enrolled in the registration books. A voter may not, under the provisions of this bill, change his party on a primary day but must stick to the party in which he is enrolled.

If improperly enrolled or if changing his party, he may request the election official to re-register him on election day, thus placing himself in position to vote for candidates of his newly chosen party at the following primary election. The voter may change his affiliation on any day since the last date of registration. Persons just reaching the voting age may be registered on election day.

Further provides that the positions on the primary ballot must be signed only by persons enrolled in the party to which the candidate aspirant belongs.

No person may write the name of a person whose name appears on another party ballot on his ticket. In cases where there are candidates, no person may have his name written on a party ballot received per his particular party.

Committees may not, under the bill, fill any vacancies outside the primary election.

Wood's second bill, which announces some time next week, provides for pre-primaries.

The convention, however, will recommend candidates and shall not, in any way, attempt to influence the result of the primary election. Any business that could be transacted in any manner would thus be limited to candidates nominated by the convention or platform.

Party conventions shall supercede the bill to be elected in upcoming primaries.

Wood's third bill is a revision and modification of the present registration laws.
